Chosen family, moral ambiguity, social margins · 2018

ShopliftersThe Work of Belonging

A thoughtful Shoplifters review from Marina’s Dreams on chosen family, poverty, performance, and Kore-eda’s compassionate moral ambiguity.

By MarinaOctober 17, 20262 min readSpoiler-light review

In this review

A Family Made in Daily RitualsWhere Care Meets ConsequenceSources & references
Film
Shoplifters
Director
Hirokazu Kore-eda
Year
2018

Shoplifters begins with a small act that feels almost like a game: Osamu and the boy Shota move through a supermarket, reading the rhythms of shelves and adult attention. Hirokazu Kore-eda makes this life on Tokyo’s margins tactile rather than sensational. The family’s cramped home is crowded with bodies, jokes, food, and overlapping voices. I was drawn to how quickly the film makes routine feel like an argument: care can be improvised, and poverty can turn ordinary errands into shared choreography.

A Family Made in Daily Rituals

The film’s most distinctive idea is not simply that family can be chosen, but that it can be performed through repetition. Meals, haircuts, small lessons, and trips to the beach become a language the household speaks together. Kore-eda observes these rituals with a patient camera and remarkably alert editing; information arrives through glances, interruptions, and things left unsaid. The result is an intimacy that never depends on a speech explaining everyone’s past. We learn the household by watching how its members make room for one another.

That warmth is carried by an ensemble that understands understatement. Lily Franky gives Osamu a loose, persuasive charm, while Sakura Ando lets Nobuyo’s guarded face register pressures she cannot easily name. The children are not treated as symbols of innocence; they have habits, calculations, and sudden flashes of authority. Even the room’s noise matters: laughter and television chatter soften the harder edges of the story, then make the silences feel newly exposed. The performances create a family before the plot asks us to define one.

Kore-eda also refuses to make theft morally decorative. The household’s tenderness exists beside exploitation, evasion, and the harm caused by keeping children outside ordinary protections. That tension is the film’s ethical strength: it asks me to understand people without turning understanding into acquittal. Its social criticism stays close to wages, housing, schooling, and the humiliations of being overlooked. Rather than announcing a position, Shoplifters makes every act of care feel entangled with a cost someone else may eventually pay.

Where Care Meets Consequence

The restraint can become a limitation. Because the film withholds context for so long, some relationships initially feel arranged to preserve mystery rather than discovered as fully lived histories. Its gentle surface may also make structural hardship seem more picturesque than it is, especially when domestic pleasures gather in beautiful, sunlit fragments. Still, the delayed storytelling suits Kore-eda’s larger purpose. The question is not whether these people fit a legal definition, but why legality and affection have been made to pull so far apart.

What stays with me is the film’s attention to touch: a hand guiding a child, bodies pressed together in a small room, a look that asks for permission without using words. Shoplifters never claims that love repairs everything. Instead, it shows how temporary belonging can be real, and how the memory of it can alter the meaning of loss without explaining away the damage. I admire a film willing to hold compassion, accountability, and hard-won trust in the same frame, without making either one easy.
